description.narrative: The first "track-1.5" Workshop on Western Indo-Pacific Security was co-hosted by the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) and the foreign policy think tank of the London School of Economics and Politics (LSE IDEAS). It took place in partnership with the Near East & South Asia Centre for Strategic Studies (NESA) of the US National Defence University. The Western Indo-Pacific (WIP) region - largely comprising the four sub-regions of southern and eastern Africa; the Horn of Africa and the Gulf region; the Arabian Sea region; and island territories - remains neglected within the larger geographical framework, in contrast to the central or the eastern Indo-Pacific regions. In this context, there were three objectives for the workshop: 1) To bring together the best of our academic and policy practitioners' minds to unpack this important and neglected WIP region; 2) To seek better ways in which the WIP could respond to these challenges and to advance pragmatic steps toward better intra-regional cooperation and coordination; 3) To help improve western and other major powers responses to the WIP region.

This cooperation and cross-cultural experience reflects the coalition framework exemplified in todays global security environment. This blend of multi-cultural experience enhances the guided discussion delivery method that comprises the majority of in-class curriculum.

title.narrative: Aviation Leadership Program (ALP)

description.narrative: The Aviation Leadership Program (ALP) provides pilot training, related training and information exchange to air force personnel in allied developing states to support their aviation expertise and defense institution building. Authorized by Section 1178 of the National Defense Authorization Act of FY 1994 and reinforced by Defense Department Directive Number 2010.12, ALP is a U.S. Air Force-funded program. In coordination with the State Department and the Defense Security Assistance Agency, the Air Force submits countries for approval of training. The Unified Combatant Commands are also permitted to submit a list of prioritized countries to receive training. Additional training permitted under this authority includes language training and programs necessary to promote better awareness and understanding of the democratic institutions and social framework of the United States. The law also allows the provision of clothing and supplies to the trainees, as well as a living stipend. The program promotes U.S. national security interests and improves bilateral relations with recipient countries.

title.narrative: NESA Center Executive Seminar 01-21: "Unseen Opponents: the Security Challenges of Pandemics

description.narrative: These flagship courses seek to stimulate dialogue on strategic issues affecting the Near East South Asia region among national security professionals. This seminar looked at pandemics: Human history reveals how societies have sought to overcome the challenges created by pandemics. The spread of bubonic plague through much of Eurasia, the influenza epidemic of the early 20th century, and smallpox outbreaks throughout much of North and South American during the 17th and 18th centuries are all cases in point. In our time, the COVID-19 outbreak created scores of challenges throughout the world. This course examines the security implications of pandemics. Not only how society can and should prepare for them, but how such incidents require an examination of 2nd and 3rd order effects. How do states address public health, while also making sure to maintain economies and to maintain positive relations with other states?

title.narrative: NESA Center Executive Seminar 03-22: "Managing New Technology and Security"

description.narrative: This course seeks to stimulate dialogue on new threats to the countries in the NESA region, and beyond. National security strategies are now addressing issues such as cyber-attacks on military and civilian infrastructures, the challenges of e-government security, managing developments in artificial intelligence, and even the use of space as a theater of security. The reality is that there is often little cooperation across borders among the countries in the NESA AOR, or even globally, to address these issues. How can states better incorporate technology into the security domain that might sometimes exceed their very capacity to do so? What, besides increased trust among partner or neighboring states is necessary to address these challenges? This seminar will look at both technological and policy implications of such cooperative measures. Ideally, participants will have a working knowledge of the use of technology in security within their country.

description.narrative: On 14 February 2024, the NESA Center for Strategic Studies held a Washington Seminar Discussion at the Army-Navy Club in Washington, D.C.
